tone_statements.citation: Akumbu, Pius W. & Roland Kießling. 2023. Variation in Central Ring: Convergence or divergence? Linguistic Typology at the Crossroads 3(1): 19–42. Bologna: University of Bologna.
tone_statements.quote: As in the Ring and Momo sub-groups of Western Grassfields Bantu generally, noun class prefixes (NPx) in Central Ring languages have high tone underlyingly. However, Babanki singles itself out as the only Ring language that rather has L tone NPx, matching with EGB, as well as Narrow Bantu where NPx have low tone (Akumbu and Hyman 2017: 1–2). [...] In isolation, the high tone in these noun prefixes is generally lowered to mid, as is shown in Table 3, while the low tone in Babanki noun prefixes is maintained as such without being affected by any further lowering.
tone_statements.locator: p. 23, section 2.1 'Low tone in noun class prefixes', with Table 3 'NPx tone of nouns in isolation' (Bum column)

tone_statements.citation: Akumbu, Pius W. 2019. Noun class 9/10 tone in Central Ring Grassfields Bantu: An overview. In Pius W. Akumbu & Esther P. Chie (eds.), Engagement with Africa: Linguistic essays in honor of Ngessimo M. Mutaka, 1–13. Köln: Rüdiger Köppe. (author version on HAL hal-03691772)
tone_statements.quote: CRGL distinguish two underlying tones, L(ow) and H(igh). On the surface, they have a level low tone (Lo) contrasting with the normal, falling L tone, but only before pause. In addition, a M(id) tone occurs in all the languages while Babanki also has a downstep (ꜜH) entity. ... High tone roots, on their part, cause downstep of the suffix H in class 10 as in Babanki (18a), or create a M tone as in Kom (18b) and Bum (18c) ... In Bum and Kung, the H prefix goes onto the root in both the singular and plural forms creating a falling tone
tone_statements.locator: p. 4, sec. 4 'Class 9/10 tone', first paragraph; after '.. ': p. 10, sec. 4.2 before ex. (18) and p. 11, sec. 4.2 before ex. (21)
tone_statements.summary: Two underlying tones, L and H, stated for the seven Central Ring languages incl. Bum; surface M in all (in Bum a suffix H lowered by a floating L) and falling HL tones in Bum; floating class 9/10 prefix tones.

tone_statements.citation: PHOIBLE 2.0, inventory 1575 'Bum (GM)' (contributor Green & Moran), source: Hedinger, Robert. 2005. Proposed Bum orthography statement. CABTAL Cameroon (unpublished).
tone_statements.quote: We have identified [6] surface tones in Bum: 3 level tones, high [aæ], mid [a‘] and low [a∆]; and 3 contour tones, low-high rising [a¿], high-low falling [a»], and high-mid falling [aÅ]. Of these six, however, only three are frequent and in contrast with each other: high, low and falling. [...] Since we have only three basic tone contrasts, we propose a tone marking system that is the same as for the neighboring Kom language: low tones are marked by the grave accent, falling tones are marked by the circumflex accent; and high, mid and rising tones are left unmarked
tone_statements.locator: section 3 Tone and 3.1, printed p. 5; Table III 'Bum Lexical Tones' and minimal pairs, printed p. 6
tone_statements.check: quotation from the author's open copy, read 2026-09-25; not yet verified by a second reading
tone_statements.summary: Tone language: six surface tones (H, M, L level; LH rising, HL falling, HM falling), three contrastive (H, L, HL falling); mid and rising 'rare', high-mid falling 'only one word' (Table III, p. 6). Minimal pairs given only among H/L/falling (p. 6). Syllabic homorganic nasal prefixes 'as far as we have been able to find out, carry a low tone' (p. 2), so left unmarked; 'one-third of vowel prefixes h

sources.citation: Andrason, Alexander & Pius W. Akumbu. 2024. Conative animal calls in Babanki and Bum (Grassfields languages of Cameroon). Kervan – International Journal of Afro-Asiatic Studies 28(1): 3–28.
sources.note: Nothing on stress or accent anywhere in the 27-page PDF (a full-text search for stress/accent/prominence: zero hits). Treats Bum as a tone language (Table 1 IPA forms carry H/L tone marks; p. 21 speaks of 'tonal patterns'). Its literature paragraph (p. 4) is the useful thing: 'Bum, in contrast, still lacks systematic studies. The only works that we are aware of comprise of brief discussions of the nominal system (Hyman 1980; Akumbu 2009), a preliminary study of the verb phrase (Bangsi 2016; see also Noumbi 1981), and a dictionary of some 1,800 entries (Ndokobaï, Hedinger, and Akumbu 2023).'
sources.venue: Kervan – International Journal of Afro-Asiatic Studies

sources.note: Section 2.1 'Low tone in noun class prefixes' (pp. 22-24): noun class prefixes in Central Ring languages (Bum included) are underlyingly H, unlike Babanki (L); in isolation the prefix H is lowered to M; Table 3 'NPx tone of nouns in isolation' gives Bum forms for the four Ring tone classes H1(HH) ū-fwɛ́n 'leg', H2(HL) ū-kpɛ̂n 'arm', L1(LH) ī-wɔ᷇ŋ 'spear', L2(LL) fū-kâk 'tree', i.e. M prefixes, H, HL-falling and other contour root tones; the authors argue the prefix H spread onto L roots producing HL contours across CR before lowering to M (after Hyman 2005). Section 3 on Bum itself is segment…
